A bullock is a male bovine (cattle) that has been castrated — meaning its reproductive organs have been surgically removed. More specifically, it is typically a young castrated male.

To put it plainly: think of a bull. Now imagine that same animal has had a simple surgical procedure done on it early in life that removes its ability to reproduce. The result is called a bullock.
Why This Is Done — and What It Changes

This might seem like an odd thing to do, but farmers have been doing it for thousands of years because it produces several very practical benefits:

1. Behaviour becomes much calmer.
A full bull is an aggressive, unpredictable, and powerful animal. It is driven by hormones and can be dangerous to handle. Once castrated, the animal loses that hormonal drive almost entirely. A bullock is noticeably gentler, more obedient, and far safer to work with.

2. The animal becomes useful for labour.
Because of that calmness, bullocks were historically used as draught animals — animals that pull heavy loads. They would pull ploughs through fields, haul carts loaded with goods, and do all the heavy physical work that required a large, strong, but controllable animal. In many parts of the world, including India, bullock carts have been a fundamental part of rural life for centuries.

3. The meat quality improves.
For farmers raising cattle for beef, castrated animals tend to put on weight more efficiently and produce meat with better texture and flavour than uncastrated bulls. So many male calves that are not needed for breeding are castrated and raised as bullocks for beef.
How a Bullock Fits Among Other Cattle

This is where many learners get confused, so it helps to see the distinctions clearly:

  • A cow is an adult female bovine that has given birth at least once.
  • A heifer is a young female bovine that has not yet given birth.
  • A bull is an uncastrated adult male bovine. It is kept for breeding.
  • A calf is any very young bovine, male or female.
  • A bullock is a castrated young male bovine — it can no longer breed, and it will never grow into a full bull.
  • A steer means exactly the same thing as a bullock. "Steer" is the word more commonly used in North America (the United States and Canada), while "bullock" is more commonly used in British, Australian, and South Asian contexts.

So if you see the word "steer" in an American book and "bullock" in a British or Indian context, they are referring to the same type of animal.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

In farming and agriculture: Any discussion of cattle farming — whether for beef, for dairy, or for agricultural labour — is likely to mention bullocks.

In South Asian daily life: If you live in India or nearby countries, the word is very familiar in the context of farming villages and rural transport. The bullock cart (a cart pulled by one or two bullocks) remains a common sight and a deeply rooted part of agricultural culture.

In livestock markets and trade: When cattle are bought and sold, bullocks are treated as a separate category from bulls and cows because their purpose and value are different.

In literature and history: Older texts, particularly those describing rural life, agriculture, or the history of work, frequently mention bullocks because before motorised engines existed, bullocks were one of the primary sources of power for hard physical labour.

In everyday spoken language — particularly in Australia, New Zealand, and parts of South Asia — people sometimes use "bullock" loosely to refer to any large young male bovine, even if it has not been castrated. This is an informal, less precise use of the word. However, in precise, technical agricultural language, a bullock is specifically a castrated young male.

If you ever encounter the word in a context where the castration detail doesn't seem relevant (say, someone is simply describing a herd), they are most likely using it in the broader sense of "a young male bovine." But the accurate, strict definition — the one used in dictionaries and professional farming contexts — always refers to castration.

A bullock is a male bovine that has been castrated, making it calm, manageable, and useful either for physical labour or for beef production. It is the same animal that Americans call a steer. You will most commonly encounter the word in farming, rural life, livestock trade, and historical or literary descriptions of agricultural societies.
